title: Center
summary_theology: A prayer for undivided devotion to Jesus that recalls Mary at his feet and the tension between serving and sitting with him, then offers the whole life for Christ's glory.
practical_worship_leadership: Works as a response after preaching on the supremacy of Christ or as a settling song early in a set. Its single focus is its strength, so pair it with a song carrying wider content and avoid stacking it with two other slow adoration songs.
arrangement_tips: Suggestions to test, since no audio was analyzed for this page. Try a full pass with the thinnest accompaniment to learn whether the melody carries on its own, set a counted length for any instrumental space, and agree an ending cue in rehearsal because slow devotional songs often end by accident.
editorial_markdown:
## What "Center" means

The song is a prayer for simplicity, asking that Jesus be the one thing a crowded life is arranged around. Its second verse recalls Mary choosing to sit at Jesus' feet while the work of the house went on, and it feels the pull between serving him and being with him without treating either as wrong. Then it offers the whole life for Christ's glory. When you introduce it, name that tension plainly. Most people in your room serve somewhere, and the song gives them a way to put their attention on Jesus himself before, during and after the serving.

## What this song does in a room

Place it after preaching on Luke 10 or on distraction, or as the settling song when a set has moved quickly and the room needs one object of attention. It also suits a volunteer commissioning, since it honors service while pointing past it. Its limit is scope. It does not survey who God is or tell the gospel story, so pair it with a song that does.

## What this song is saying about God

A prayer for undivided devotion to Jesus that recalls Mary at his feet and the tension between serving and sitting with him, then offers the whole life for Christ's glory.

## Scriptural backbone

Read Luke 10:38-42, where Jesus receives both sisters and commends Mary's choice of attention without dismissing Martha's hospitality. Read Colossians 1:17-18 for Christ holding everything together and having first place, which grounds the offer of a whole life. Psalm 27:4 voices one desire, to be near the Lord and look on his beauty, and gives you a short reading before the first verse.

## How to use it in a service

The listed length of the live track runs near eight minutes. If your slot is shorter, decide before rehearsal which sections you will keep, how many times the chorus returns, and whether one repeated section gets a quieter pass with the band pulled back. Write that order on every chart and in the lyric software so repeats are decisions. Plan a clear ending cue, because a slow devotional song with an open tail often ends by accident.

## Things to watch for as the worship leader

The resource for this page is the live recording from the Bethel Music album We Must Respond, with Abbie Gamboa leading. MultiTracks lists the recording key as A on its [resource page](https://www.multitracks.com/songs/Bethel-Music/We-Must-Respond/Center-(Live)/overview/). That key belongs to the recording. This page recommends no congregational key, because no melody range has been measured for it. Sing the chorus with the vocalist who will lead and move the key only if the high phrases strain or the low phrases vanish in your room.

## A note for the team behind you (techs, vocalists, band)

Test each of these in your room before trusting it. Ask the vocalist to speak the chorus text at tempo before singing it, so phrasing is deliberate. Have the band play a full pass with the thinnest possible accompaniment to learn whether the melody carries on its own, then add parts back one at a time. Set a count for any instrumental space, so the congregation knows when to breathe and when to sing. Confirm the lyric operator has the agreed repeat count in writing.

The recording reference is Bethel Music with Abbie Gamboa, Center (Live) from We Must Respond, on [MultiTracks](https://www.multitracks.com/songs/Bethel-Music/We-Must-Respond/Center-(Live)/overview/), checked October 28, 2026. The listed key and length belong to that live version only. Writers listed are Brian Johnson, Abbie Gamboa and Gabriel Gamboa. Before Sunday, have your leader read Luke 10:38-42 aloud at rehearsal and choose the sentence that introduces the song.

title: AMAZING!
summary_theology: An energetic confession of rescue from sin and shame through the cross and resurrection of Jesus, celebrating new life received as a gift rather than earned.
practical_worship_leadership: A high-energy opener or a celebration after baptisms, testimony or a resurrection sermon. Introduce it as a song about what Christ has done rather than a report that everyone in the room already feels free, so grieving people are not shut out.
arrangement_tips: Suggestions to test, not observations of the record. Run it once at a slower click to lock lyric rhythm before bringing it to speed, watch for rushing on repeated choruses, and settle the ending as a cold stop or held chord with the drummer before Sunday.
editorial_markdown:
## What "AMAZING!" means

This is a gospel confession sung at celebration pace. The text tells of rescue from sin and shame through the cross and resurrection of Jesus, and it insists that the new life it describes was received and never earned. The exclamation in the title is the response to that rescue. When you introduce it, point at what Christ did rather than at how the room should feel, so the shout has an object. The song declares a finished work. It does not promise that every weight lifts in the first chorus, and you should not promise that either.

## What this song does in a room

Use it to open a service, follow a baptism, or respond to a testimony of conversion. It belongs on Easter and on any Sunday the sermon lands on grace. Its limit is that a fast declaration of rescue can sound like a verdict on everyone's week, so say in one sentence that the song is about what Jesus did, and let people join at the volume they have.

## What this song is saying about God

An energetic confession of rescue from sin and shame through the cross and resurrection of Jesus, celebrating new life received as a gift rather than earned.

## Scriptural backbone

Read Ephesians 2:4-9, where God in mercy makes the dead alive with Christ and salvation is a gift and never a wage, which matches the song's confession of new life received. Read Romans 6:4 on being raised with Christ to walk in new life, useful on a baptism Sunday. Psalm 103:10-12 describes sin removed as far as east is from west, a quiet reading before a loud song.

## How to use it in a service

Fast songs expose indecision faster than slow ones. Settle the number of verses and chorus repeats before rehearsal and write them on the chart, along with where any instrumental break falls and how long it lasts. Decide whether the song ends cold or on a held chord, and give the drummer the cue. Check any chart's section order against your own agreed form before it reaches the lyric software.

## Things to watch for as the worship leader

The recording for this page is the ELEVATION RHYTHM recording with Josiah Queen on the WASHED album. MultiTracks lists the recording key as Gb on its [resource page](https://www.multitracks.com/songs/ELEVATION-RHYTHM/WASHED/AMAZING!/overview/). Treat that as a fact about the record. No congregational key is recommended here, since melody range has not been measured. Test the chorus at the listed key with your actual lead vocalist, and with two or three untrained singers if you can, then transpose if the loudest section sits where ordinary voices thin out.

## A note for the team behind you (techs, vocalists, band)

These are suggestions for rehearsal, and your room will decide which hold. Run the song once at a slower click to lock the lyric rhythm, then bring it to the listed tempo. Ask the band to listen for rushing on repeated choruses, the common failure at this speed. Have the lead vocalist practice the title line so the energy comes from clean diction rather than volume. Check that the lyric operator can keep pace with short repeated lines.

The recording reference is ELEVATION RHYTHM with Josiah Queen, AMAZING! from WASHED, on [MultiTracks](https://www.multitracks.com/songs/ELEVATION-RHYTHM/WASHED/AMAZING!/overview/), checked October 28, 2026. The listed key and tempo apply to that recording only. Writers listed are Joshua Holiday, Josiah Queen, Zac Lawson and Steven Furtick. Before rehearsal, write the one sentence that names the rescue, and have the band hear it before the count-in.

title: THANK GOD I'M FREE
summary_theology: Expressive thanksgiving for forgiveness and Christ's completed work, using cleared-debt imagery and admitting that the singer could not have accomplished salvation alone.
practical_worship_leadership: Suits a thanksgiving service, a baptism celebration, or an early-set song to get the room moving. Frame the gratitude as thanks for what Christ has secured so people who are grieving or stuck can still sing it.
arrangement_tips: Suggestions to test. Compare the chorus with drums alone and with full kit to decide how much drive your room needs, try the title line as a statement rather than a shout, and rehearse the tempo transition from whatever song precedes it.
editorial_markdown:
## What "THANK GOD I'M FREE" means

The song ties loud, bodily thanks to one specific cause, the forgiveness Christ finished. Its picture is a debt cleared and a record wiped, and it admits that the singer could never have done that work alone. So the freedom is legal before it is emotional, and the dancing is a response to a settled account. Teach it that way. Freedom from sin's charge is true for the believer on a hard morning as much as a good one, and the song does not claim that addiction, grief or illness vanish when the chorus starts.

## What this song does in a room

Open a service with it, close a baptism with it, or use it on a Sunday the sermon reaches forgiveness. Its strength is a clear reason for joy. Its limit is participation pressure. Some people cannot or will not move, and some are grieving, so invite movement without requiring it and keep your introduction on what Christ cleared rather than on how the room looks.

## What this song is saying about God

Expressive thanksgiving for forgiveness and Christ's completed work, using cleared-debt imagery and admitting that the singer could not have accomplished salvation alone.

## Scriptural backbone

Read Colossians 2:13-14, where the record of debt that stood against us is cancelled and nailed to the cross, the closest match for the song's imagery. Read Psalm 32:1-2 on the blessing of forgiven sin and a covered record. Luke 15:22-24 shows a father who orders celebration for a returned child, which frames dancing as a response to being received.

## How to use it in a service

Decide how many times the title line returns and where the energy peaks. Fast thanksgiving songs often work as a shortened form early in a set and a longer form as a closer, so choose which slot you are filling and build the form for it. Mark the ending, since a repeated title line can loop past the point where the congregation is still singing. Write the agreed form on the chart and in the lyric file.

## Things to watch for as the worship leader

The recording for this page is the ELEVATION RHYTHM track with Lizzie Morgan on the WASHED album. MultiTracks lists the recording key as E on its [resource page](https://www.multitracks.com/songs/ELEVATION-RHYTHM/WASHED/THANK-GOD-I%27M-FREE/overview/). The listing tags the track as a female lead, which describes the recording and says nothing about who should sing it in your church. No range has been measured for this page and no congregational key is recommended. Run the chorus with your actual leader and move the key if the top sits out of reach for the room.

## A note for the team behind you (techs, vocalists, band)

Try the following and keep what works in your room. Build the chorus in stages at rehearsal, first voices with one rhythm instrument, then add bass and drums, then the full band, and stop at the stage where the congregation can still hear itself sing. Ask the vocalist to try the title line as a statement and then as a shout, and compare which the congregation picks up faster. Rehearse the transition into the song from whatever precedes it, since a jump from a slower song needs a counted click or a spoken bridge.

The recording reference is ELEVATION RHYTHM with Lizzie Morgan, THANK GOD I'M FREE from WASHED, on [MultiTracks](https://www.multitracks.com/songs/ELEVATION-RHYTHM/WASHED/THANK-GOD-I%27M-FREE/overview/), checked October 28, 2026. The listed key and tempo apply to that recording only. Writers listed are Joshua Holiday, Tiffany Hudson, Mitch Wong and Sydney James. At rehearsal, agree one sentence that invites movement without requiring it, and have the leader say it over the intro.

title: What a God
summary_theology: A testimony of grace that meets failure and seeks the lost without requiring perfection, settling into satisfaction in God himself even when nothing visible has changed.
practical_worship_leadership: Use it to lift the congregation's eyes before a sermon on God's nature or as a slower adoration song after a faster opener. Pair it with a testimony or reading that gives a concrete act of God, since attribute songs can feel abstract on their own.
arrangement_tips: Suggestions to test. If two vocalists share the lead, have each sing the chorus alone in the listed key before deciding whether one key serves both, practice the exact beat of each hand-off, and decide the ending in rehearsal so neither leader has to call it on stage.
editorial_markdown:
## What "What a God" means

Despite the title, this is a song about grace meeting failure. Its verses voice surprise that God comes toward people who have fallen short and goes looking for those who are lost, with no demand that they first become acceptable. Its later sections settle into contentment in God himself, even when nothing visible has changed. So the exclamation is about character revealed in rescue, and the ending is about having enough in him. Teach it as a testimony song. The congregation names what God did when they failed, then says he is enough while they wait.

## What this song does in a room

Use it after preaching on the prodigal, on Peter's restoration, or on contentment, and in any service where people have been invited to admit failure. It suits a response slot more than an opener because its weight sits in the later sections. Its limit is that it does not survey God's attributes in general, so a sermon on majesty or creation will want a different song.

## What this song is saying about God

A testimony of grace that meets failure and seeks the lost without requiring perfection, settling into satisfaction in God himself even when nothing visible has changed.

## Scriptural backbone

Read Luke 15:1-7 and 15:20-24, where the shepherd searches for one sheep and the father runs toward a returning son, the pattern of God seeking the lost that the verses describe. Read Habakkuk 3:17-19, where the prophet rejoices in God with empty fields and stalls, a match for finding satisfaction without visible intervention. Philippians 4:11-13 adds learned contentment.

## How to use it in a service

The listed length is a little over seven minutes. If your slot is shorter, choose whether to keep the verses about being met in failure, the later sections about contentment, or both, and set a chorus count. Decide the ending in rehearsal, since a testimony song that settles into contentment can run longer than planned.

## Things to watch for as the worship leader

The recording for this page is the SEU Worship track with ONE HOUSE on the album Move of God. MultiTracks lists the recording key as A on its [resource page](https://www.multitracks.com/songs/SEU-Worship/Move-of-God/What-a-God/overview/) and tags both female and male lead vocals on the track. Those details describe the record. No congregational key is recommended here, because melody range is unmeasured. Sing the chorus at the listed key with whoever will lead it and move the key if the later sections sit where the room cannot hold them.

## A note for the team behind you (techs, vocalists, band)

Try these and keep what works. Have the lead vocalist sing the chorus alone at the listed key to hear where it sits. Ask the band to play a verse with a single harmonic instrument so the words about failure and grace are heard, then build back. Rehearse the move into the later sections so the shift from testimony to contentment is deliberate. Confirm the lyric operator knows which repeats are planned.

The recording reference is SEU Worship with ONE HOUSE, What a God from Move of God, on [MultiTracks](https://www.multitracks.com/songs/SEU-Worship/Move-of-God/What-a-God/overview/), checked October 28, 2026. The listed key and tempo belong to that recording, and the official SEU chart lists the same values. Writers listed are Bobby Walker, Brunes Charles, Chelsea Plank, Kenzie Walker and Roosevelt Stewart. Before Sunday, have the leader write one sentence about being met in failure to introduce it.

title: TAKEOVER
summary_theology: A prayer of Spirit-led surrender with breath, wind and fire imagery, offering the singer's life as God's dwelling and hoping for revival without manufacturing it.
practical_worship_leadership: Fits a response time after a sermon on the Spirit, a consecration moment, or a prayer set. Lead it as an invitation people may enter at their own pace and avoid promising what the Spirit will do in the next ten minutes.
arrangement_tips: Suggestions to test. Hold a chorus at the quietest sustainable level and check the vocal still reads, try the title word as a plea rather than a command, and rehearse the silence after the final chord so nobody fills it by reflex.
editorial_markdown:
## What "TAKEOVER" means

The song is a surrender prayer. With images of breath, wind and fire, it asks the Spirit to lead, and it offers the singer's life as a place for God to live and work. It also looks forward to revival and to miracles. The title describes yielded agency, a person handing the wheel to God on purpose, and it does not describe a loss of self. Keep two things distinct when you lead it. The lyric's hope for God to move is a prayer the church may pray. A promised outcome, or a required physical response, is something you cannot add.

## What this song does in a room

Use it as a response after a sermon on the Spirit, at a consecration or commissioning, or inside a prayer set where people are asked to yield something named. Its limit is pressure. A surrender song can be led as a demand for visible reaction, so introduce it as a prayer people may pray where they stand, and let the hope for revival stay a hope rather than a schedule.

## What this song is saying about God

A prayer of Spirit-led surrender with breath, wind and fire imagery, offering the singer's life as God's dwelling and hoping for revival without manufacturing it.

## Scriptural backbone

Read Romans 8:9-14, where the Spirit dwells in believers and leads God's children, which fits a life offered as God's dwelling. Read Romans 12:1-2 on presenting the body as a living sacrifice and being transformed. Acts 1:8 and 2:1-4 give the wind and fire imagery its setting, with power promised for witness rather than for display.

## How to use it in a service

Surrender songs depend on everyone knowing where the end is. Decide how many passes the chorus gets, whether there is a stripped section where the band drops out, and how you will signal the close. Write the form on the chart and share it with the person running lyrics and the person praying after the song. Leave room for a short spoken prayer if your tradition does that, and give it a planned length.

## Things to watch for as the worship leader

The recording for this page is the ELEVATION RHYTHM track on the WASHED album. MultiTracks lists the recording key as F on its [resource page](https://www.multitracks.com/songs/ELEVATION-RHYTHM/WASHED/TAKEOVER/overview/). That key belongs to the record. This page recommends no congregational key, because no range has been measured. Sing the chorus at the listed key with the vocalist who will lead and move it if the low phrases drop out of hearing or the peak phrases strain.

## A note for the team behind you (techs, vocalists, band)

Test each of these in your room before trusting it. Have the band hold a single pass of the chorus at the quietest level they can sustain and check that the vocal still reads. Ask the vocalist to try the title word as a plea and then as a command, and listen to which lands as prayer. Rehearse the silence after the last chord so nobody fills it by reflex. Confirm the pastor or prayer leader knows the cue to speak.

The recording reference is ELEVATION RHYTHM, TAKEOVER from WASHED, on [MultiTracks](https://www.multitracks.com/songs/ELEVATION-RHYTHM/WASHED/TAKEOVER/overview/), checked October 28, 2026. The listed key and tempo describe that recording only. Writers listed are Mitch Wong, Jonathan Stamper and Joshua Holiday. Before rehearsal, agree with the prayer leader how the song ends and what is said next, and write both on the chart.

title: Wild Rushing Wind
summary_theology: A welcome to the Spirit's presence using wind, rain and fire imagery, asking for renewal and expecting freedom and change as a prayer of faith.
practical_worship_leadership: Works in a prayer set, at Pentecost, or before a time of waiting on God. Introduce it as asking and avoid promising that the wind will blow on cue, so the room is not set up for disappointment or performance.
arrangement_tips: Suggestions to test. Play a verse with rhythm only to see whether the melody holds without harmonic support, give any open prayer section a time limit and a cue to resume, and rehearse who ends the song when it moves into silence.
editorial_markdown:
## What "Wild Rushing Wind" means

This is a welcome and a request. The text greets the Spirit's presence with images of wind, rain and fire and asks for renewal, and it expects that freedom and change will follow. The expectation is faith rather than a demand. When you teach it, let the congregation ask for renewal with full confidence that God answers, while making clear that nobody has to prove the answer by what they feel in the next ten minutes. The Spirit's work is real whether or not a room notices it at once.

## What this song does in a room

Use it at Pentecost, in a prayer set, or before a time of waiting on God after preaching on renewal or repentance. It also fits a service that begins a new ministry year. Its limit is that its hope for change can be turned into a feelings test, so introduce it as a request God is pleased to receive and leave the evidence to him.

## What this song is saying about God

A welcome to the Spirit's presence using wind, rain and fire imagery, asking for renewal and expecting freedom and change as a prayer of faith.

## Scriptural backbone

Read Acts 2:1-4 for the wind and fire at Pentecost, a preparation parallel rather than a script for what must happen again. Read John 3:5-8, where the Spirit moves like wind that cannot be tracked, which keeps expectations humble. Titus 3:5-6 names the washing of renewal by the Spirit poured out through Jesus, which matches the song's rain imagery and ties renewal to Christ.

## How to use it in a service

Decide the shape before rehearsal, with the chorus count, any extended prayer section, and the ending written down. If you plan a section where the band holds and the room sings freely, give it a time limit and a cue to resume. Share the form with the lyric operator and with whoever leads prayer after it. Check any chart's section order against your own decisions before it reaches the screen.

## Things to watch for as the worship leader

The recording for this page is the SEU Worship live track from Found In The Field. MultiTracks lists the recording key as D on its [resource page](https://www.multitracks.com/songs/SEU-Worship/Found-In-The-Field/Wild-Rushing-Wind-(Live)/overview/). Treat that as a fact about the record. No congregational key is recommended here, since range is unmeasured for this page. Run the chorus at the listed key with your lead vocalist and move it only after hearing where the highest sustained phrase lands for the people in the pews.

## A note for the team behind you (techs, vocalists, band)

These are suggestions for rehearsal, and your room will decide which hold. Have the band play a verse with rhythm only to see whether the melody holds without harmonic support, then restore parts. Ask the vocalist to sing the title phrase at two intensities and pick the one the congregation can match. Practice the moment you move from the song into silence or prayer so the band knows who ends it. Confirm the audio engineer knows the dynamic plan.

The listed key applies to that live version only. Writers listed are Caylie Bryant, Austin Davis and Jonathan Gamble. At rehearsal, set a time limit for any open prayer section and agree who cues the band back in.

title: WELCOME HOME
summary_theology: An invitation to return to the Father and receive Jesus as salvation, celebrating reconciliation with God through family, home and new-creation imagery.
practical_worship_leadership: Strong fit for baptisms, membership Sundays, guest-focused services and Luke 15 sermons. Frame the home as the Father's house rather than a family ideal, since some in the room have homes that are not safe or prodigals who have not returned.
arrangement_tips: Suggestions to test. Lock the groove with drums and bass alone before adding parts, build a labeled long form with a re-entry point if the song runs under baptisms, and rehearse the hold section at a steady level for a full minute to check for drift.
editorial_markdown:
## What "WELCOME HOME" means

The song is an invitation to come back to the Father and to receive Jesus as salvation, and it celebrates that return with family, home and new-creation imagery. Home here means reconciliation with God. It is more than a friendly building and more than a song about heaven later. When you lead it, let the welcome be the gospel welcome your church teaches, offered through repentance and faith, so the words carry assurance for those who have come and an open door for those who have not. Nobody is told they are already home without being asked to come.

## What this song does in a room

Use it at baptisms, on a guest-focused Sunday, after preaching on Luke 15 or 2 Corinthians 5, and at membership services. It can also close an evangelistic service if a response is offered. Its limit is false assurance. A room full of visitors should hear the invitation clearly, so pair it with a spoken call rather than letting the chorus do the pastor's work.

## What this song is saying about God

An invitation to return to the Father and receive Jesus as salvation, celebrating reconciliation with God through family, home and new-creation imagery.

## Scriptural backbone

Read Luke 15:11-24 for the father who runs to meet a returning son and calls for a feast. Read 2 Corinthians 5:17-21, where anyone in Christ is a new creation and God pleads through his people to be reconciled, which fits the new-creation imagery. Ephesians 2:17-19 describes strangers made members of God's household.

## How to use it in a service

Decide the chorus count and where the energy peaks, then write it down. Celebration songs tend to gain repeats on stage, so set a limit and assign the person who calls the ending. If you plan to use it during baptisms, build a longer looping form with a clear re-entry point so the band can hold while people come out of the water. Give the lyric operator the long form and the short form, labeled.

## Things to watch for as the worship leader

The recording for this page is the ELEVATION RHYTHM track with SEU Worship on the WASHED album. MultiTracks lists the recording key as F on its [resource page](https://www.multitracks.com/songs/ELEVATION-RHYTHM/WASHED/WELCOME-HOME/overview/). That key belongs to the recording. This page recommends no congregational key, because range has not been measured. Sing the chorus at the listed key with the vocalist who will lead, and move it if the congregation's attempts at the top phrases go quiet.

## A note for the team behind you (techs, vocalists, band)

Test these in your room before trusting them. Have the drummer and bass run the chorus alone to lock the groove, then add the rest. Ask the vocalist to try the title phrase as something said to a person and listen for whether diction improves. Rehearse the hold section with the full band at a steady level for a full minute to make sure it does not drift. Confirm the baptism team knows the cue to begin.

The listed key and tempo describe that recording only. Writers listed are Chelsea Plank, Joshua Holiday, Kenzie Walker and Steven Furtick. Before Sunday, agree with your pastor what spoken invitation follows or precedes the song and who gives it.

title: All The Glory
summary_theology: A throne-room song in which elders, creatures, angels and the redeemed honor Jesus as slain Lamb and king, drawing on the scroll and priestly kingdom of Revelation 4 and 5.
practical_worship_leadership: Use as a closing declaration, a communion response, or the praise song after a sermon on the cross or on heaven. Plan for the room to hear itself, since proclamation songs lose the congregation when the band carries all the weight.
arrangement_tips: Suggestions to test. Have the vocalist sing the chorus unaccompanied for the band, try one chorus with only drums and voices to find out whether the congregation could carry it, and ask the engineer to leave headroom for a loud final chorus.
editorial_markdown:
## What "All The Glory" means

The song sets the congregation inside the throne room. Elders, living creatures, angels and the redeemed stand together honoring Jesus as the Lamb and as king, with the scroll and a redeemed kingdom of priests in view. So the title is a line in that heavenly scene, and the room sings as part of the crowd. Teach it that way. Your people are joining a worship already in progress rather than generating their own, and the glory goes to the Lamb because he was slain and has purchased people for God.

## What this song does in a room

Use it to close a service, at communion, on Easter or Ascension, and after preaching on Revelation 4 and 5 or on Christ's reign. It also suits all-church gatherings where the point is joining a larger worship. Its limit is that it is a throne-room song and not a general gratitude song, so it wants a place where the Lamb's victory has already been named.

## What this song is saying about God

A throne-room song in which elders, creatures, angels and the redeemed honor Jesus as slain Lamb and king, drawing on the scroll and priestly kingdom of Revelation 4 and 5.

## Scriptural backbone

Read Revelation 4:8-11 and 5:6-14, the throne, the scroll, the Lamb who was slain, and the song of the redeemed from every nation made a kingdom and priests. Those chapters supply nearly every image in the lyric. Read John 1:29 for the first naming of Jesus as Lamb of God. Hebrews 12:22-24 reminds the congregation that they have already come to that gathering.

## How to use it in a service

Pick the verses you will keep, set the chorus count, and decide whether any proclamation section repeats with the band pulled back so the congregation leads. Mark the ending, and if your slot is shorter than the listed length decide which sections to cut before rehearsal. Write the form on the chart and in the lyric file. Check any chart's section sequence against your plan before it reaches the screen.

## Things to watch for as the worship leader

The recording for this page is the Bethel Music live track with John Wilds on the album All The Glory. MultiTracks lists the recording key as G on its [resource page](https://www.multitracks.com/songs/Bethel-Music/All-The-Glory/All-The-Glory-(Live)/overview/). Treat that as a fact about the record. No congregational key is recommended here, since no range has been measured. Run the chorus at the listed key with your leader and check whether the most repeated phrase sits where an untrained voice can hold it.

## A note for the team behind you (techs, vocalists, band)

Try these and keep what works. Have the vocalist sing the chorus unaccompanied so the band hears the melody they are supporting. Try one chorus with only drums and voices to find out whether the congregation could carry it, then rebuild. Ask the audio engineer to leave headroom for a loud final chorus so the mix does not clip when the room sings. Confirm the ending cue with the drummer.

title: For Christ Alone
summary_theology: Jesus' unique mediation, ransom, cross and resurrection joined to a life committed to the gospel, rejecting idols and awaiting his return, with commitment as response rather than condition.
practical_worship_leadership: Fits Easter, a sermon on Christ's return, a commissioning service, or any gathering where the congregation declares whom they belong to. Place it after honest prayer so a confident register does not sound triumphalist.

## What "For Christ Alone" means

The song joins what Jesus alone has done to how the singer now lives. It names his unique place between God and people, his ransom, his cross and his resurrection, then commits the whole life to the gospel, rejects idols, and looks for his return. The order matters. Commitment follows atonement as a response, and nothing the singer promises adds to what Christ finished. Teach it as a pledge of allegiance from people who have already been rescued, and keep the pledge from sounding like a condition of the rescue.

## What this song does in a room

Use it on Easter, at commissioning and ordination services, on a Sunday about Christ's return, or when a sermon confronts idols. Its limit is register. A pledge sung with confidence can sound triumphant on a morning when the room is tired, so place it after honest prayer and let the ransom and cross carry the weight before the commitment lines.

## What this song is saying about God

Jesus' unique mediation, ransom, cross and resurrection joined to a life committed to the gospel, rejecting idols and awaiting his return, with commitment as response rather than condition.

## Scriptural backbone

Read 1 Timothy 2:5-6, one mediator between God and humanity who gave himself as a ransom, which matches the song's claim of unique mediation. Read Colossians 1:18-20 on Christ as head of the church with first place in everything, reconciling all things by his cross. ## What "NEED YOU" means

The song begins where honest prayer begins, approaching God on mercy and not on merit. ## What this song does in a room

Use it at communion, on Good Friday, during a season of repentance, or as the opening prayer of a service where people are asked to be honest. ## What "Good Plans" means

This is Psalm 23 sung as trust. The text walks through the shepherd, the valley of the shadow of death, the rod and staff, goodness and mercy following, and the house of the Lord as home. The good plans of the title are the shepherd's, and they run through the valley rather than around it. Teach it with that psalm open. The song does not promise a preferred job, a healthy bank balance or a life without loss. It promises a shepherd who stays, and it keeps trusting while the distress continues.

Use it after preaching on Psalm 23, at funerals and memorial services, in seasons of transition, and in a prayer set for people facing decisions or diagnoses. Its limit is misreading. ## Scriptural backbone

Read Psalm 23 in full, since the song draws its shepherd, valley, rod and staff, pursuing goodness and mercy, and the Lord's house from it. title: He Shall Be Praised
summary_theology: Present praise joined to enduring heavenly and earthly praise, naming Jesus as Lion and Lamb and holding resurrection hope in trouble, with movement offered as invitation.
practical_worship_leadership: A mid-tempo praise song for opening a set, following a baptism, or closing with a declaration. Plan dynamics on purpose, since a steady declaration feels static when every section sits at the same level.

editorial_markdown:
## What "He Shall Be Praised" means

The song joins the praise of this moment to praise that does not end, on earth and in heaven, and it names Jesus as both Lion and Lamb. Its hope is resurrection hope, held in the middle of trouble rather than after it. The title's future tense is the point. Praise is owed and will be given, whatever the week has been, so a congregation can sing it as a statement of fact on a weak morning. The text includes clapping and movement language, which is an invitation and never a test of sincerity or ability.

## What this song does in a room

Use it to open a set, to follow a baptism, or to close a service on a declaration. It fits sermons on Revelation 5, on perseverance, and on resurrection. Its limit is participation pressure. If you call for clapping or standing, say that people may join as they are able, so the praise stays about Jesus and not about who moved.

## What this song is saying about God

Present praise joined to enduring heavenly and earthly praise, naming Jesus as Lion and Lamb and holding resurrection hope in trouble, with movement offered as invitation.

## Scriptural backbone

Read Revelation 5:5-6, where the Lion of Judah is seen as a Lamb who was slain, the pairing the song uses. Read Psalm 113:2-3 on the Lord's name praised from sunrise to sunset and forever. 1 Peter 1:3-7 ties living hope through the resurrection to trials that test faith, which matches praise held in trouble.

## What "REASONS" means

The reason for praise in this song is a person. The text points to Jesus himself as the ground for worship through trials, names forgiveness and resurrection hope, and keeps returning to mercy that does not run out. It is a list with one item that keeps unfolding, and it is a different song from 10,000 Reasons. Teach it so the congregation hears that trouble does not cancel the reason, since the reason is Christ and not circumstance. Celebration and grief can share this song in the same room.

## What this song does in a room

Open a service with it, use it after testimonies, or sing it on a Sunday when the sermon has moved through suffering to hope. Its limit is pace and pressure together. The quantity in the title is the language of a grateful person rather than a measurement of blessings owned. Teach it as gratitude rooted in Christ's work, so that when the congregation sings about how much has been given, the cross and the empty tomb are what they mean.

title: At The Altar
summary_theology: A flawed and broken life offered in response to grace, using altar imagery for surrendered worship and bringing fear and anxiety to God without promising relief or requiring movement.
practical_worship_leadership: Suits a response time after preaching, an altar call where your tradition uses one, a consecration service, communion, or a stewardship Sunday framed as worship. Lead it as an open invitation people may answer where they sit, without pushing anyone forward.

editorial_markdown:
## What "At The Altar" means

The song brings a flawed and broken life to God in response to grace, and it uses the altar as a picture of surrendered worship. What is laid down includes dreams and victories as well as failures, and the text speaks openly about fear and anxiety. Lead that language with care. The altar is where a person brings what frightens them to God. It is not a promise that symptoms stop, and nobody should be shamed because theirs continue. The altar also needs no furniture and no walk forward. People can offer the whole of themselves where they sit.

## What this song does in a room

Use it as a response after preaching, at a consecration or dedication service, at communion, or on a Sunday about anxiety where pastoral care is also on offer. Its limit is pressure and promise. Do not require movement, and do not pair it with claims of instant relief. Let it be the moment people hand God what they carry.

## What this song is saying about God

A flawed and broken life offered in response to grace, using altar imagery for surrendered worship and bringing fear and anxiety to God without promising relief or requiring movement.

## Scriptural backbone

Read Romans 12:1-2 on presenting the body as a living sacrifice, the clearest parallel to altar worship offered in response to mercy. Read 1 Peter 5:6-7 on humbling oneself under God's hand and casting anxiety on him because he cares. Psalm 51:17 reminds the room that a broken and contrite heart is a sacrifice God receives.

## How to use it in a service

Build a Sunday form by choosing the sections that carry the offering content and setting a chorus count. If the song supports a response time, prepare a looping form with a marked re-entry so the band can hold while people pray or come forward. title: Move of God
summary_theology: A prayer for the Spirit's action in church, city, family and personal life, including repentance, idol removal and renewed hunger, waiting on God rather than on intensity.
practical_worship_leadership: Fits a prayer night, a vision Sunday, Pentecost, or a season of asking for renewal. Lead it as desire that the Spirit answers in his own time, and avoid turning it into a demand that something visible happen in the next ten minutes.

## What "Move of God" means

The song asks God to act, and it is specific about where, in the church, the city, the family and the singer's own life. Its request includes repentance and the removal of idols, renewed hunger for God, and a willingness to wait for him. So it is a revival prayer with a cost attached, and the cost lands first on the people singing. Teach it that way. The congregation is asking to be changed rather than asking for a show, and the waiting language in the text means waiting on God rather than waiting for the room to reach a certain volume.

## What this song does in a room

Use it at prayer nights, on a vision Sunday, at Pentecost, and in a season when the church is asking for renewal. It also fits sermons on 2 Chronicles 7 or on repentance. Its limit is manipulation. Extending the song does not secure an encounter, and nobody should feel kept in their seat until something is felt, so agree a responsible ending and keep it.

## What this song is saying about God

A prayer for the Spirit's action in church, city, family and personal life, including repentance, idol removal and renewed hunger, waiting on God rather than on intensity.

## Scriptural backbone

Read 2 Chronicles 7:14, where God's people humble themselves, pray, seek his face and turn from wickedness, the shape of the song's request. Read Acts 4:29-31, a church praying for boldness and receiving the Spirit's filling. Psalm 85:4-7 asks God to revive his people so they may rejoice in him, a prayer the room can borrow.

## How to use it in a service

Decide the chorus count and where any extended prayer section falls. If you plan a time where the band holds and people pray aloud, give it a time limit and a clear cue to resume. ## What "What A Worthy Name" means

The song moves through the whole story of Jesus, his coming in flesh, his cross, his rising, his place above all things, and his reign that does not end. The church's confidence in the song rests on him alone. The title is the response to that story, so when you lead it, keep the story in view and the name will carry its weight. It is a separate song from What A Beautiful Name, with its own writers and melody, and the version on this page is the live Passion 2026 recording.

## What this song does in a room

Use it on Easter, at communion, on Christ the King Sunday, and after preaching on Colossians 1 or Philippians 2. It also works as a creed-shaped closer when a service has covered the gospel. Its limit is that a slow song reciting the story needs a room that already knows it, so place it after the reading or the sermon.

## What this song is saying about God

Honoring Jesus' incarnation, cross, resurrection, preeminence and lasting reign, with the church's confidence resting in him alone, and distinct from What A Beautiful Name.

## Scriptural backbone

Read Colossians 1:15-20, where Christ is the image of God, firstborn from the dead, holding first place and reconciling all things by his cross, which maps the song's movement. Read Philippians 2:6-11 on humbling to death and the name above every name. Acts 4:12 says salvation is found in no other name.

## How to use it in a service

editorial_markdown:
## What "What Kind Of God" means

The song starts at the incarnation and asks what kind of God would come so low, then follows Jesus into service and to the cross, and it ends with the singer offering thanks and self in return. Its bridge adapts material from the carol What Child Is This, so your congregation will hear something familiar inside a new song. The resource on this page is a distinct composition with its own modern verses and chorus, and the carol relation should be named in your planning rather than discovered mid-service. Teach it as a Christmas song that keeps walking from the manger to the cross.

## What this song does in a room

Use it in Advent, at Christmas Eve candlelight services, and at a Christmas-season communion, where its movement to the cross and self-offering fits the table. It also serves any service on the humility of Christ. Its limit is familiarity. If your church already sings What Child Is This, decide whether the two sit together or compete.

## What this song is saying about God

From incarnation and humility to service, the cross and thankful self-offering, with a bridge that adapts What Child Is This material inside a distinct modern composition.

## Scriptural backbone

Read Philippians 2:6-8, where Christ empties himself, takes the form of a servant, and humbles himself to death on a cross, the path the song walks. Read Luke 2:1-20 for the birth, the manger and the shepherds. Mark 10:45 adds that the Son of Man came to serve and to give his life, which joins the manger to the cross.

## How to use it in a service

Decide which verses to keep, whether the bridge drawn from What Child Is This stays, and how many times the question returns. For a candlelight service, build a shorter form that fits between readings, and for a Sunday in Advent build a fuller one. title: Another Like You
summary_theology: Adoration of God's fullness revealed in Jesus, remembering mercy at the cross, inviting to the table with body and blood imagery, and honoring the reigning Lamb alongside his faithfulness.
practical_worship_leadership: Fits a communion response, a slow adoration slot after preaching, or a service built around God's faithfulness through a hard season. Place it after the reason for adoration has been named, since a long slow song can lose an unprepared room.

editorial_markdown:
## What "Another Like You" means

The song praises God for the fullness of who he is as revealed in Jesus. It remembers mercy at the cross, it invites the singer to the table with body and blood imagery, and it honors the Lamb who now reigns. Faithfulness is recalled alongside redemption, so the comparison in the title rests on acts, since no one else has done this. Teach it as a communion-shaped adoration song. The room is naming what God has done in Christ and finding no rival, and the table imagery means it belongs near the bread and cup more than at the top of a set.

## What this song does in a room

Use it at communion, on Maundy Thursday, on Good Friday evening, and after preaching on the cross or on God's faithfulness through a hard season. Its limit is sacramental overreach. Singing it does not do what your church teaches the table does, so let it prepare people for the meal within your own teaching rather than stand in for it.

## What this song is saying about God

Adoration of God's fullness revealed in Jesus, remembering mercy at the cross, inviting to the table with body and blood imagery, and honoring the reigning Lamb alongside his faithfulness.

## Scriptural backbone

Read Colossians 1:19-20 and 2:9, where the fullness of God dwells in Christ and peace is made by his blood. Read Luke 22:19-20 for the body given and the cup of the new covenant, which the song's table imagery recalls. Micah 7:18 asks who is a God like you, pardoning sin and delighting in steadfast love.

## How to use it in a service

Choose the verses that carry the cross and mercy content and set a chorus count. title: Midst

practical_worship_leadership: Fits the opening of a set as a call to worship, a Pentecost service, or a prayer gathering where God's presence is named before anything is asked. Lead it as a statement of promise so the congregation can sing it on a flat morning without pretending.

editorial_markdown:
## What "Midst" means

The song asks for awareness of God's presence and for the Spirit's work, with imagery of fire, flood, whisper and wind, and it prays in the language of the Lord's Prayer for God's kingdom to come. The request is for attention surrendered, not for God to arrive from somewhere else. He is already among his people by promise. Teach it that way. Volume, visible excitement and particular manifestations are not the measure of his presence, and the music does not summon him. The congregation asks to notice and to yield, and to see his kingdom come where they live.

## What this song does in a room

Use it to open a set as a call to worship, at Pentecost, at a prayer gathering, and after preaching on the Lord's Prayer or on 1 Kings 19. Its limit is the temptation to equate presence with intensity. Lead it as a prayer of attention, and let a flat morning still count as a morning God is present.

## What this song is saying about God

A request for awareness of God's presence, surrendered attention and the Spirit's work, with fire, flood, whisper and wind imagery and a kingdom-come petition, never equating presence with intensity.

## Scriptural backbone

Read Matthew 6:9-10, where Jesus teaches his disciples to pray for the Father's kingdom to come and his will to be done on earth, the petition the song echoes. Read 1 Kings 19:11-13, wind, earthquake and fire, and then a low whisper, which matches the song's imagery and its humility. Matthew 18:20 promises Jesus among those gathered in his name.

## How to use it in a service

Decide the chorus count and whether a section repeats with the band pulled back so the congregation carries the declaration. Mark the ending, since a live presence song can extend in ways your Sunday slot cannot. If you use it as a call to worship, build a shorter form that hands off cleanly to the next song.
